title: The miner in the build server
summary: Brightloom Games' build server has run at full CPU all night. Trace a brute-forced CI login to a script console, a dropper, three kinds of persistence and a cryptominer talking to a mining pool, then clean up and rebuild.
ctf: One of the attacker's ways back in carries a flag in its comment (step 7). Submit it on the CTF board as "The miner in the build server".

playbook.trigger: The build server's CPU stays at 100% or calls out to a mining pool
decisions: Rebuild the server or clean it in place?
targets: Remove all three ways back in the same day
notify: CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing it (2022 Directions)
done: Rebuilt from a known good image

template.s:
# Incident runbook: the miner in the build server

08:30, Thursday 5 Nov. Monitoring says **build01** at **Brightloom Games** has been above 95% CPU for six hours, and developers say game builds take 38 minutes instead of 6. build01 runs Forgeway CI, a Jenkins-style build server. You are on call.

The evidence is in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python). The network tools (`nmap`, `curl`, `wget`, `tshark`, `dig`, `nslookup`, `host`, `whois`, `ping`, `traceroute`, `nc`, `ssh`, `openssl`, `nikto`, `gobuster`) work on a recorded copy of the case network; nothing leaves your browser.

The steps follow the incident response lifecycle: **verify, scope, find the way in, preserve evidence, contain, eradicate, recover, learn**. The order is based on the open LetsDefend incident response playbooks (MIT licence).

### What you'll learn

- Spot a cryptominer hiding behind a kernel thread's name
- Prove a brute force on a CI login, and why a script console is a remote shell
- Find three kinds of Linux persistence: cron, systemd and SSH keys
- Follow mining traffic to a pool and contain, eradicate and rebuild

### How to use this runbook

- Run a cell with **Shift+Enter** (or its Run button). Run the cells in order: the first Linux cell copies the evidence into `~/case`.
- Tick each `- [ ]` box when you have done it.
- Stuck? Open a **Hint** under the step.
- Type your answer into each **check** box and it tells you if you are right. Answers are short: an address, a name, a number or a time such as 09:05.
- Write your notes under each step. Download .ipynb keeps your notes and every output.

## 1. Triage

- [ ] Write your name and the time you started here:
- [ ] Hash the evidence before you touch it
- [ ] Read the alert, then map the network

> Hint: `sort -t, -k2 -n` sorts a CSV by its second column. Or read cpu_metrics.csv from the top and find where the numbers jump.
?> How many hosts does `nmap -sn 10.60.0.0/24` find up? :: sha256:4b227777d4dd1fc61c6f884f48641d02b4d121d3fd328cb08b5531fcacdabf8a
?> At what time (HH:MM) did CPU first go above 90%? :: sha256:8dc525a190e6749d30d6548bd1b26bf2b45be8d46a6bbe7feda7274e30299e6f

cd ~/case

## 2. Verify: is this real?

Alerts are often wrong. Before you wake anyone up, decide whether this is a **true positive**.

- [ ] What exactly raised the alarm, and when?
- [ ] Name two pieces of evidence that prove something bad really happened
- [ ] What harmless explanation would make this a false positive? Can you rule it out?
- [ ] Decision: true positive / false positive (write it here)

On Linux, real kernel threads such as `kswapd0` show in `ps` with square brackets and use almost no CPU. A program in `/var/tmp` with the same name is a disguise.

> Hint: Compare the two kswapd0 lines in ps.txt: who runs them, where they live, and how much CPU they use.
> Hint: ss.txt shows which program owns each network connection.
?> What is the PID of the fake kswapd0? :: sha256:0315b4020af3eccab7706679580ac87a710d82970733b8719e70af9b57e7b9e6
?> Which remote TCP port is the fake kswapd0 connected to? :: sha256:318aee3fed8c9d040d35a7fc1fa776fb31303833aa2de885354ddf3d44d8fb69

grep -E 'kswapd0|java|PID' ps.txt
echo ---
grep -E 'kswapd0|State' ss.txt
echo ---
cat suspect/config.json

## 4. Initial access: the login page

- [ ] Count the failed sign-ins and find the address they came from
- [ ] Which username was guessed, and when did a guess work?
- [ ] Why didn't the server stop it after ten tries?

> Hint: A failed sign-in is `POST /j_security_check` with status 401. A working one gets 302 (a redirect to the dashboard).
> Hint: ci_audit.log names the user. The 2024 lines explain why the password was weak and never locked.

## 5. From login to shell: the script console

A CI server's script console runs any code on the server, as the CI user. Admin on a CI server means a shell on the box, and access to every secret the builds use.

- [ ] What did the attacker run through the console? List both scripts
- [ ] Which secrets file did they read? What lives in it (Git tokens, cloud keys, signing keys)?
- [ ] Where did the dropper script come from?

> Hint: `grep script-console ci_audit.log` shows each script. The second one downloads and runs a shell script with `curl | sh`.
?> Which file of secrets did the attacker print through the console? (file name) :: sha256:aaa36223768b459a0161f26b020f1751de14d09644fc839eb50621ac69913668
?> Which IP address served x.sh? :: sha256:bfeb4c6192985efa05e7fa0740ac45708a515e569e7edaec7fc060ff72b44a0c

grep -E 'POST /script|GET /script' ci_access.log
echo ---
grep script-console ci_audit.log
echo ---
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http.request and ip.src==10.60.0.12' -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e ip.dst -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

## 6. Read the dropper and the miner

Read `x.sh` line by line. Never run malware to see what it does; read it.

- [ ] Which competing miners does it kill first?
- [ ] Which files does it download, and where does it hide them?
- [ ] How does it become root? What is in `persist/sudoers.d_forgeway`, and why was it added?
- [ ] What do the strings say the "kswapd0" program really is?

> Hint: `sudo -n` runs a command as root only if no password is needed. The sudoers line explains why that worked.
?> Which account ran sudo to install the persistence? :: sha256:58a9c8b6d18f81ba65b14f875e415bfd2a60e2a474d2721fc28bd2170c0ee1a9
?> Which sudoers keyword let it become root without a password? :: sha256:c797f6834c354fedaee9e19bd52583f73ee2255bea1d6cc412168eff78675c99

cat -n suspect/x.sh
echo ---
cat persist/sudoers.d_forgeway
grep sudo auth.log
echo ---
head -3 suspect/kswapd0.strings.txt
echo ---
sha256sum suspect/* | while read h f; do
    grep -q "$h" known_bad.txt && echo "KNOWN BAD: $f" || echo "not listed: $f"

## 7. Persistence: every way back in

Attackers rarely leave one way back. If you remove one and miss another, the miner is back in 15 minutes.

- [ ] The cron file: how often does it re-download x.sh?
- [ ] The systemd service: what does it start, and what happens if you kill the process?
- [ ] The SSH keys: which key doesn't belong? Was it used? (A CTF flag is in the key's comment.)
- [ ] The forgeway user's own crontab: is it clean?

> Hint: In cron, `*/15` in the minute field means every 15 minutes. In systemd, `Restart=always` brings a killed process back.
> Hint: Compare the two keys in root_authorized_keys. Then grep auth.log for root logins.
?> How many different persistence mechanisms did the attacker add? :: sha256:4e07408562bedb8b60ce05c1decfe3ad16b72230967de01f640b7e4729b49fce
?> What is the file name of the attacker's systemd unit? :: sha256:81cb95987259a90a2551ba28d64bcf1dd5f5bc84c6df07b66c2e435cc282e2ba
?> At what time (HH:MM) did the attacker log back in as root over SSH? :: sha256:08218c866bbd592e8f89e9f88fea496ce0d092cc4e7d58510173b23df13818ff

for f in persist/*; do echo "== $f"; cat "$f"; done
echo ---
grep -E 'publickey for root|sysupdate' auth.log

- [ ] Which name did build01 look up just before mining started?
- [ ] What does the first message to port 3333 contain? (stratum `login` with a wallet)

## 9. Who is behind it?

- [ ] What is the dropper host, and when was its domain registered?
- [ ] Look up the wallet on the pool: how many machines mine for it? What does that tell you about the campaign?
- [ ] Who should get an abuse report?

In a real case, ask before you touch an attacker's servers: it can tip them off, and some actions are illegal. Looking up a public pool page is fine.

> Hint: The wallet is in suspect/config.json. Put it at the end of the pool's /api/wallet/ address.

## 10. Initial access: how did they get in?

The way in is the door you must close, or it happens again. Tick the one the evidence supports, and write the evidence next to it.

- [ ] Phishing (a message that tricked someone)
- [ ] Exploit of a public-facing application (a website or service bug)
- [ ] Valid accounts (a real username and password or key, stolen or misused)
- [ ] External remote services (VPN, remote desktop, SSH)
- [ ] Drive-by compromise (a booby-trapped website)
- [ ] Supply chain or trusted partner
- [ ] Hardware added (a USB device or rogue machine)
- [ ] Insider using access they were given
- [ ] No intrusion (for example, traffic from outside that never got in)

## 11. Preserve the evidence

Cleaning up destroys evidence. Copy everything to a safe place, record the hashes and pack it before you change anything.

- [ ] Copy the evidence and write SHA256SUMS
- [ ] Note who collected it, when, and where it is stored (chain of custody)

> Hint: Collect before you clean. Once you delete the cron file and kill the miner, that evidence is gone forever.

mkdir -p ~/evidence && cp -r ~/case/* ~/evidence/
cd ~/evidence && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS -exec sha256sum {} + > SHA256SUMS
pack=~/evidence-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M).tar
tar cf "$pack" -C ~/evidence .
(gzip -f "$pack" 2>/dev/null && echo "packed $pack.gz") || echo "packed $pack"
ls -l ~/evidence-*
wc -l SHA256SUMS
cd ~/case

## 12. Contain

- [ ] Remove the port forward so the CI server is no longer on the internet
- [ ] Block the dropper host, the pool and the attacker address
- [ ] Disable the admin account and end its sessions
- [ ] Revoke every secret in credentials.xml now: assume they are stolen

The cell prints the commands for the real systems. Nothing here touches a real firewall.

> Hint: Contain the way in first (the port forward), then the outbound paths (pool and dropper), then the stolen secrets.

echo "firewall nat delete ci.brightloom.test:8080"
for ip in 203.0.113.99 198.51.100.23 198.51.100.77; do
    echo "iptables -A OUTPUT -d $ip -j DROP"
    echo "iptables -A INPUT -s $ip -j DROP"
done
echo "dns-block add hashmoat.example"
echo "dns-block add sysupdate-mirror.example"
echo "forgeway-cli disable-user admin --kill-sessions"
echo "rotate: every token and key in /var/lib/forgeway/credentials.xml"
template.e:
firewall nat delete ci.brightloom.test:8080
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 203.0.113.99 -j DROP
iptables -A INPUT -s 203.0.113.99 -j DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 198.51.100.23 -j DROP
iptables -A INPUT -s 198.51.100.23 -j DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 198.51.100.77 -j DROP
iptables -A INPUT -s 198.51.100.77 -j DROP
dns-block add hashmoat.example
dns-block add sysupdate-mirror.example
forgeway-cli disable-user admin --kill-sessions
rotate: every token and key in /var/lib/forgeway/credentials.xml

template.s:
## 13. Eradicate

Remove all three ways back in, then the miner. Order matters: stop the service and the cron entry before you kill the process, or they start it again.

- [ ] Remove the cron file and the systemd unit
- [ ] Remove the attacker's SSH key, keep the real one
- [ ] Delete the miner and its config
- [ ] Remove the NOPASSWD sudo rule

> Hint: `grep -v` prints every line that does NOT match, so it keeps the good key.

echo "systemctl disable --now sysupdate.service"
rm -f persist/etc_cron.d_sysupdate persist/sysupdate.service
grep -v Hq7mXbV0 persist/root_authorized_keys > /tmp/keys && mv /tmp/keys persist/root_authorized_keys
echo 'forgeway ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/docker' > persist/sudoers.d_forgeway
rm -f suspect/config.json
echo "kill 4242; rm -rf /var/tmp/.cache"
echo ---
ls persist
cat persist/root_authorized_keys
template.e:
systemctl disable --now sysupdate.service
kill 4242; rm -rf /var/tmp/.cache
---
crontab_forgeway.txt  root_authorized_keys  sudoers.d_forgeway
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIMd2Pz8kQwErTy5uIoPa3SdFgHjKl9ZxCvBnM1qW2eRt ops@brightloom.test

## 14. Recover

A server where someone was root can't be fully trusted again. The safe path is to rebuild it.

- [ ] Rebuild build01 from a clean image and restore only the job configs
- [ ] Put Forgeway behind the VPN, with single sign-on and MFA; lock accounts after failed sign-ins
- [ ] Give the CI user only the sudo it needs (or none: run builds in containers)
- [ ] Watch: CPU on build servers, outbound connections to port 3333, new cron files and systemd units

> Hint: Builds were 6x slower. Check that build times are back to normal after the rebuild: that is your recovery test.

## 15. Report

- [ ] Timeline from 01:49 to 08:30 with sources
- [ ] Root cause: internet-facing CI, weak admin password, no lockout, NOPASSWD sudo
- [ ] Indicators: addresses, domains, wallet, file hashes, SSH key
- [ ] Submit the flag from step 7 on the CTF board

Write the report here. Download .ipynb keeps every output above.

## 16. Lessons learned

- [ ] How did the attack happen, start to finish?
- [ ] What went well in the response?
- [ ] What would you do differently next time?
- [ ] Which fixes stop it happening again? Who owns each one, and by when?
- [ ] Which early warning signs should be watched from now on?
